patient.name: Liam Doherty
patient.setting: Hostel in Camden, then ambulance and Emergency Department resus
patient.complaint: Found unresponsive and barely breathing by hostel staff
background: Known heroin use; recently released from prison
Ate a takeaway an hour before

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' or 'most likely cause?' with an unresponsive patient who is not breathing but has a pulse, often with pinpoint pupils (opioids) or signs after intubation (oesophageal tube).

points: Hostel staff find Liam slumped on his bed at 22:00.
He does not respond to voice or pain.
A used syringe lies on the floor.

steps.q: Liam is not breathing adequately but has a carotid pulse of 54. What is this?
steps.r: Not breathing **with a pulse** is respiratory arrest. Cardiac arrest has **no pulse**.

steps.lead: Liam still has a pulse, but without breathing his oxygen will run out and his heart will stop next.

visual.title: Respiratory rate
visual.label: Liam 3/min
visual.caption: A rate of 3 is not effective breathing: treat as respiratory arrest.

steps.lead: Liam is **apnoeic** in all but name: unresponsive, minimal chest movement, cyanosed, SpO2 71% and GCS 3.
Pinpoint pupils plus slow breathing in a heroin user: **opioid overdose**. Later in resus, watch for the other signature, **oesophageal intubation**.
Opioids are one of many causes; others include choking, sedatives, alcohol, severe asthma, COPD, brainstem stroke and head injury.

steps.text: Do not start chest compressions on someone with a **pulse**. Ventilate, and check the pulse every 2 minutes in case it is lost.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which investigation confirms correct tracheal tube placement?' (capnography) and 'Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?' (ABG) after the airway is secured.

points: Liam vomits in the ambulance; GCS stays 3.
In resus the team decides to **intubate**.
Because he has just eaten, an **LMA** is not suitable.
After the tube goes in, SpO2 **falls to 79%**.
No breath sounds at either lung base.
His **abdomen swells** with each squeeze of the bag.

steps.q: Which test confirms whether Liam's tube is in the trachea?
steps.r: **Capnography**: exhaled CO2 only comes from ventilated lungs. A flat trace means the tube is in the oesophagus.

steps.lead: Liam's capnograph shows **no CO2 waveform**: the tube is in his oesophagus. It is removed, he is re-oxygenated and re-intubated.

visual.title: End-tidal CO2 after intubation
visual.caption: A trace that fades to zero is oesophageal; a sustained trace is tracheal.

steps.title: Arterial blood gas (after re-intubation, on 100% O2)
steps.text: Acute respiratory acidosis: CO2 has built up while he was not breathing.

steps.lead: Liam's **ABG** shows how poorly he ventilated; a **toxicology screen** and paracetamol level are sent because overdose is suspected.

steps.text: Low SpO2 + absent air entry at both bases + a **distended abdomen** after intubation = oesophageal tube until capnography proves otherwise.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?': open the airway (jaw thrust if C-spine risk), ventilate with oxygen, and give IV naloxone if opioids are the cause.

steps.title: Unresponsive, not breathing normally, pulse present
nodes: Open airway: head tilt-chin lift (jaw thrust if C-spine)
Check pulse; treat the cause (naloxone for opioids)
steps.caption: Airway, breathing, then the cause.

steps.q: Liam was found on his bed with no trauma. How should the paramedic open his airway?
steps.r: No neck injury, so **head tilt-chin lift**. Jaw thrust is used when **cervical spine** injury is a concern.

steps.lead: Liam's airway is opened, vomit suctioned, an **oropharyngeal airway** inserted, and he is ventilated by **bag-valve mask** with high-flow oxygen.

steps.q: He is being ventilated and still has a pulse. Which drug now?
steps.r: **Naloxone** reverses opioid respiratory depression. Naltrexone is for relapse prevention; flumazenil is for benzodiazepines.

steps.lead: Liam gets **IV naloxone 400 micrograms** while ventilation continues. A sedation-related airway obstruction would instead need an airway adjunct.

steps.text: Naloxone wears off faster than many opioids. Keep watching: Liam may **re-sedate** and need repeat doses or an infusion.

steps.lead: Liam's care follows the **Resuscitation Council UK** basic life support and airway guidance: airway, ventilation, pulse check, then the cause.

steps.text: In a non-fasted patient a **laryngeal mask** gives poor protection from aspiration: a cuffed tracheal tube is safer.

science.exam: Expect applied mechanism questions: why opioids stop breathing (mu receptors in the brainstem), why capnography works, and why respiratory arrest leads to cardiac arrest.

steps.lead: Heroin acts on **mu-opioid receptors** in Liam's brainstem, so rising CO2 no longer drives him to breathe.

steps.q: Why did Liam's heart rate fall to 54 before treatment?
o: Direct opioid toxicity to the SA node
steps.r: Progressive **hypoxaemia** starves the myocardium, causing bradyarrhythmias and then cardiac arrest.

steps.lead: Left alone, Liam's falling oxygen and rising CO2 would have slowed his heart into arrest.

steps.title: From respiratory to cardiac arrest
steps.caption: The usual pattern in children, whose arrests are mostly respiratory first.

steps.lead: Liam's floppy, unconscious pharynx let his tongue fall back: the same reason **sedated** or anaesthetised patients need an airway adjunct.
Only Liam's lungs return CO2, so a tube in his oesophagus showed **no end-tidal CO2**.
Every minute Liam was hypoxic risked **brain injury**: the reason fast airway opening and ventilation matter most.

steps.text: Bradycardia in a hypoxic child is a **pre-arrest** sign: fix the airway and oxygenate first.

mcq.q: What is the key clinical difference between respiratory arrest and cardiac arrest?
o: Cyanosis is absent in respiratory arrest
GCS is normal in respiratory arrest
A pulse may be present in respiratory arrest
Pupils are dilated in respiratory arrest
mcq.r: In respiratory arrest a **pulse may still be present**; cardiac arrest has no pulse.

mcq.q: Which triad after intubation suggests oesophageal intubation?
o: Low SpO2, absent basal air entry, distended abdomen
Low SpO2, unilateral air entry, tracheal deviation
mcq.r: Low SpO2, **no air entry at both bases** and a **distended abdomen**.

mcq.q: Pinpoint pupils with slow breathing most suggest which cause?
mcq.r: **Opioid overdose** gives miosis and respiratory depression.

mcq.q: Why is a laryngeal mask airway unsuitable in a non-fasted patient?
o: It cannot be used with oxygen
It gives poor protection against reflux of gastric contents
mcq.r: An **LMA** does not seal the airway against **aspiration**.

mcq.q: Which investigation confirms correct tracheal tube placement?
mcq.r: **Capnography** detects end-tidal CO2, only produced by ventilated lungs.

mcq.q: Which first-line test assesses oxygenation and ventilation?
mcq.r: An **ABG** gives pO2, pCO2 and pH.

mcq.q: Which airway manoeuvre is preferred if cervical spine injury is suspected?
mcq.r: **Jaw thrust** opens the airway without moving the neck.

mcq.q: What is the antidote for opioid-induced respiratory arrest?
Which simple airway adjunct is used after general anaesthesia when tone is lost?
mcq.r: An **oropharyngeal airway** holds the tongue off the back of the throat.

mcq.q: Through which receptor do opioids cause respiratory depression?
mcq.r: **Mu-opioid receptor** agonism in the brainstem respiratory centres.

prompts.q: What is respiratory arrest and how does it differ from cardiac arrest?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: check the pulse. Pulse present = respiratory arrest.

points.p: Failure of breathing, so no oxygen delivery
points.why: Ineffective breathing (e.g. RR 3) counts too.

points.p: A pulse may still be present at first
points.why: Cardiac arrest has no pulse.

points.p: Untreated, it progresses to cardiac arrest
points.why: Through hypoxic bradycardia.

prompts.q: How does a patient in respiratory arrest look?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: unresponsive and not breathing, but the pulse is there.

points.p: Apnoea / not breathing
points.why: Look, listen and feel for no more than 10 seconds.

points.p: Unresponsive
points.why: Altered GCS from hypoxia or the cause.

points.p: Reduced or absent chest movement
points.why: See-saw movement suggests obstruction.

points.p: Cyanosis and low SpO2
points.why: Central cyanosis is a late sign.

prompts.q: What are the causes of respiratory arrest?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: sort them into airway, brain and lung.

points.p: Airway obstruction: choking, foreign body, the tongue
points.why: The tongue is the commonest cause in the unconscious.

points.p: CNS depression: opioids, sedatives, alcohol
points.why: Opioids are the classic exam cause.

points.p: Respiratory failure: severe asthma, COPD exacerbation
points.why: Tiring patients with a falling RR are about to arrest.

points.p: Neurological: brainstem stroke, head injury
points.why: Damage to the respiratory centre.

points.p: Trauma, sedation and anaesthesia
points.why: Loss of airway tone after GA.

prompts.q: Which features point to opioid overdose, and which to oesophageal intubation?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: two signature vignettes from the notes.

points.p: Opioid: pinpoint pupils
points.why: Plus track marks or a PCA pump in the stem.

points.p: Opioid: slow or absent breathing
points.why: RR often under 8.

points.p: Oesophageal tube: low SpO2
points.why: Falls after intubation.

points.p: Oesophageal tube: absent air entry at both bases
points.why: Bilateral, unlike endobronchial intubation (one side).

points.p: Oesophageal tube: distended abdomen
points.why: Air is going into the stomach.

prompts.q: Why is a laryngeal mask airway unsuitable in some patients?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: 'just eaten' or 'not fasted' in the stem.

points.p: Poor protection against reflux of gastric contents
points.why: It sits above the larynx and does not seal the trachea.

points.p: Unsuitable in non-fasted patients
points.why: Use a cuffed tracheal tube instead.

prompts.q: How do you confirm correct tracheal tube placement, and why does it work?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: not the CXR, not auscultation.

points.p: Waveform capnography
points.why: The gold standard for detecting oesophageal intubation.

points.p: CO2 is only reliably exhaled from ventilated lungs, not the oesophagus
points.why: A trace that fades to zero means the oesophagus.

prompts.q: What are the first-line investigations once the airway is secured?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the ABG measures how well they ventilate.

points.p: ABG to assess oxygenation and ventilation
points.why: Raised pCO2 with acidosis shows hypoventilation.

points.p: Bloods and toxicology screen if overdose suspected
points.why: Mixed overdoses are common.

points.p: Imaging guided by the suspected cause
points.why: E.g. CT head for head injury or stroke.

prompts.q: What are the emergency steps for an unresponsive patient who is not breathing but has a pulse?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: airway first; jaw thrust if the neck may be injured.

points.p: Call for help
points.why: Early senior and airway support.

points.p: Head tilt-chin lift, or jaw thrust if C-spine concern
points.why: Jaw thrust avoids moving the neck.

points.p: Remove visible obstruction; insert oropharyngeal airway
points.why: Do not blind finger sweep.

points.p: Ventilate: bag-valve mask (or mouth-to-mask) with high-flow oxygen
points.why: About 10 breaths a minute.

points.p: Check circulation / pulse
points.why: If the pulse is lost, start CPR.

prompts.q: What specific treatment is given in opioid-induced respiratory arrest, and what else after anaesthesia?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: naloxone does not replace ventilation.

points.p: Naloxone alongside ventilatory support
points.why: IV route acts fastest; repeat if needed as it wears off.

points.p: After GA: simple airway adjunct (oropharyngeal airway) for lost tone
points.why: Loss of airway smooth muscle tone causes obstruction.

prompts.q: Why do opioids stop breathing, and why does respiratory arrest lead to cardiac arrest?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: name the receptor and the site; then hypoxia causes bradycardia.

points.p: Mu-opioid receptor agonism in brainstem respiratory centres
points.why: Not kappa or delta.

points.p: Blunted ventilatory response to hypercapnia
points.why: Rising CO2 no longer drives breathing.

points.p: Hypoxaemia causes myocardial hypoxia, then bradyarrhythmia and cardiac arrest
points.why: Respiratory-then-cardiac pattern, especially in children.

points.p: Delay causes cerebral hypoxia and brain injury
points.why: The main reason to act fast.

glossary.Respiratory arrest: Breathing has stopped or is ineffective while the heart may still be beating.
glossary.Cardiac arrest: The heart stops pumping effectively, so there is no central pulse.
glossary.Cyanosis: Blue discolouration of lips and skin from low blood oxygen.
glossary.GCS: Glasgow Coma Scale, 3 to 15: eye, verbal and motor responses.
glossary.Pinpoint pupils: Very small (miotic) pupils, classic of opioid toxicity and pontine haemorrhage.
glossary.Naloxone: An opioid receptor antagonist that rapidly reverses opioid respiratory depression.
glossary.Naltrexone: An oral opioid antagonist used for relapse prevention, not for acute overdose.
glossary.Flumazenil: A benzodiazepine antagonist; not used for opioids.
glossary.Head tilt-chin lift: The standard manoeuvre to open the airway by tilting the head back and lifting the chin.
glossary.Jaw thrust: Lifting the jaw forward from behind its angles to open the airway without moving the neck.
glossary.Cervical spine: The neck vertebrae; injury is a concern after trauma, so the neck is not tilted.
glossary.Oropharyngeal airway: A curved plastic (Guedel) tube placed in the mouth to stop the tongue blocking the airway.
glossary.Guedel: Another name for an oropharyngeal airway.
glossary.Bag-valve mask: A hand-squeezed bag and face mask used to ventilate a patient with oxygen.
glossary.Laryngeal mask airway: A supraglottic airway that sits over the larynx; quick to insert but does not protect against aspiration.
glossary.Tracheal tube: A cuffed tube passed through the vocal cords into the trachea; seals and protects the airway.
glossary.Oesophageal intubation: A tracheal tube wrongly placed in the oesophagus, so the stomach, not the lungs, is ventilated.
glossary.Capnography: Continuous measurement and waveform of exhaled CO2; confirms the tube is in the trachea.
glossary.End-tidal CO2: The CO2 level at the end of each breath out; absent if the tube is in the oesophagus.
glossary.ABG: Arterial blood gas: pH, pO2, pCO2 and bicarbonate from an arterial sample.
glossary.Hypercapnia: A raised level of carbon dioxide in the blood.
glossary.Hypoxaemia: A low level of oxygen in the blood.
glossary.Respiratory acidosis: Low pH caused by CO2 retention from inadequate ventilation.
glossary.Mu-opioid receptor: The opioid receptor responsible for analgesia and for respiratory depression in the brainstem.
glossary.Toxicology screen: Blood or urine tests for drugs taken in overdose.
glossary.Aspiration: Inhaling stomach contents or fluid into the lungs.
glossary.PEA: Pulseless electrical activity: organised ECG rhythm but no pulse.
glossary.Track marks: Scars along veins from repeated injection drug use.
glossary.PCA: Patient-controlled analgesia: a pump that lets the patient give themselves opioid doses.
glossary.Cerebral hypoxia: Lack of oxygen to the brain, causing injury within minutes.
glossary.Re-sedation: Return of opioid toxicity once short-acting naloxone wears off.

technique.stem: A 29 year old man is found collapsed in a public toilet. He is unresponsive to pain. His pulse rate is 56 bpm, BP 98/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 2 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 70% breathing air. His pupils are pinpoint and there are track marks on both arms. His capillary glucose is 6.1 mmol/L.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis in an unresponsive patient: is there a pulse, and what is the cause?
Pulse present, breathing failed, miosis and IV drug use, normal glucose.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Respiratory arrest from opioid overdose**.

elim: Alcohol does not cause pinpoint pupils.
He has a pulse, so this is not cardiac arrest.
Glucose is normal.
No seizure activity is described.

steps.x: **D. Opioid-induced respiratory arrest.** Pulse present + RR tiny + pinpoint pupils.

technique.stem: A 58 year old woman is intubated in the Emergency Department after a respiratory arrest. After intubation her oxygen saturation falls from 90% to 78%. There is no air entry at either lung base and her abdomen becomes distended with each ventilation.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the position of the tube?

steps.x: Confirming tube position: think what is reliable and immediate.

clues: no air entry at either lung base
steps.x: The classic picture of **oesophageal intubation**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Capnography**: no exhaled CO2 means the tube is not in the lungs.

elim: ABG shows the effect, not the tube position.
Auscultation is unreliable.
CXR is slow and cannot exclude oesophageal placement.
Oximetry lags and does not show the position.

steps.x: **E. Waveform capnography.** No trace, wrong place.

technique.stem: A 70 year old man collapses in the outpatient waiting room. He does not respond to voice or pain and is not breathing. A carotid pulse is clearly palpable at 64 bpm. Help has been called. There is no history of trauma.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Airway opening with head tilt-chin lift

steps.x: 'Initial' management of an unresponsive, non-breathing patient.
Pulse present = respiratory arrest; no trauma means the neck can be tilted.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Open the airway: **head tilt-chin lift**, then ventilate.

elim: He has a pulse, so no compressions.
Defibrillation is for pulseless VF or VT.
Adrenaline is for cardiac arrest.
No clue suggests opioids; the airway comes first anyway.

steps.x: **A. Head tilt-chin lift.** Airway before anything else.

technique.stem: A 45 year old woman with cancer pain takes an extra dose of oral morphine. Two hours later she is drowsy with a respiratory rate of 5 breaths per minute and pinpoint pupils. Her arterial pCO2 is 8.9 kPa, but her breathing does not increase.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her respiratory depression?
o: Agonism at mu-opioid receptors in the brainstem
Blockade of nicotinic receptors at the neuromuscular junction

steps.x: A drug mechanism question.
An opioid with a blunted response to high CO2.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Mu-opioid receptor agonism** in the brainstem respiratory centres.

elim: Nicotinic blockade is neuromuscular blockers: she would be paralysed, not miotic.
GABA-A enhancement is benzodiazepines.
Acetylcholinesterase inhibition is organophosphates.
Chemoreceptor stimulation would increase breathing.

steps.x: **A. Brainstem mu-receptor agonism.** Reduces the drive to breathe from CO2.

practice.stem: A 62 year old man is found collapsed on a hospital ward. He does not respond to voice or pain. There are no chest movements. His pulse rate is 50 bpm and BP 94/58 mmHg; oxygen saturation is 72% breathing air. His capillary glucose is 6.4 mmol/L.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Unresponsive and not breathing with a pulse present is respiratory arrest. Cardiac arrest has no pulse.

steps.x: Diagnosis in an unresponsive patient.

clues: does not respond to voice or pain
steps.x: Not breathing, pulse present, glucose normal.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Respiratory arrest**.

elim: He has a pulse and a BP.
Glucose is normal.
No seizure activity.
A faint recovers quickly and breathing continues.

steps.x: **C. Respiratory arrest.** Pulse present, breathing absent.

practice.stem: A 71 year old woman is on day 1 after a hip replacement with morphine patient-controlled analgesia. She is found difficult to rouse. Her pulse rate is 58 bpm, BP 104/66 mmHg, respiratory rate 5 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 84% breathing air. Her pupils are pinpoint.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of her respiratory depression?
practice.e: A slow respiratory rate with pinpoint pupils on a morphine PCA is opioid toxicity, heading for respiratory arrest. PE causes tachypnoea, not bradypnoea.

steps.x: A cause question for slow breathing.
Opioid source, CNS depression, miosis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Opioid toxicity** from the PCA.

elim: Glucose is normal.
PE causes fast breathing and tachycardia.
Sepsis gives tachypnoea, fever and tachycardia.
Stroke gives focal signs, not pinpoint pupils with a PCA.

steps.x: **B. Opioid toxicity.** Stop the PCA, support ventilation, give naloxone.

practice.stem: A 55 year old man is intubated in the Emergency Department after a respiratory arrest. Five minutes later his oxygen saturation is 76% and falling. There are no breath sounds at either lung base, and his abdomen is distended. The trachea is central.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of his deterioration?
practice.e: Low SpO2, absent air entry at both bases and a distended abdomen after intubation is the classic triad of oesophageal intubation. Right main bronchus intubation gives absent breath sounds on the left only.

steps.x: A cause for deterioration just after intubation.

clues: no breath sounds at either lung base
steps.x: Bilateral absent air entry plus a filling stomach.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Oesophageal intubation**.

elim: Aspiration gives crackles and develops over hours.
Bronchospasm gives wheeze and high airway pressure, not a distended abdomen.
Right main bronchus intubation silences the left side only.
Tension pneumothorax is one-sided with tracheal deviation and hypotension.

steps.x: **C. Oesophageal intubation.** Confirm with capnography and re-intubate.

practice.stem: A 48 year old man chokes on a piece of steak in a restaurant. He clutches his throat, then becomes unresponsive. He is not breathing and his lips are blue. Paramedics arrive 2 minutes later.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
practice.e: Early in respiratory arrest from airway obstruction, the heart is still beating, so a pulse is palpable. Without treatment it will progress to cardiac arrest.

steps.x: An examination finding: think about the timeline.

clues: chokes on a piece of steak
steps.x: Airway obstruction causing respiratory arrest, seen early.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Respiratory arrest: a **pulse is still present** initially.

elim: Pulse loss comes later, once hypoxia stops the heart.
No air is moving, so no wheeze is heard.
Fixed dilated pupils suggest prolonged arrest or brain death.
Pinpoint pupils are opioids; there is no drug history.

steps.x: **D. Palpable carotid pulse.** Respiratory arrest comes before cardiac arrest.

practice.stem: A 39 year old woman is in the recovery room after a general anaesthetic. She is unresponsive and snoring loudly, then goes silent. Her chest and abdomen move in a see-saw pattern but no air is felt at her mouth. A jaw thrust immediately restores airflow. Her pulse rate is 96 bpm and BP 128/74 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of her respiratory arrest?
o: Upper airway obstruction by the tongue
practice.e: Loss of pharyngeal muscle tone under anaesthesia lets the tongue obstruct the airway: snoring, then see-saw breathing, relieved by a jaw thrust.

steps.x: A cause question after anaesthesia.
Breathing effort with no airflow: obstruction, fixed by lifting the jaw.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Upper airway obstruction** from loss of tone.

elim: Bronchospasm gives wheeze, not snoring, and jaw thrust would not fix it.
Opioids reduce effort; she is making strong efforts.
PE does not cause snoring or see-saw breathing.
Residual blockade gives weak effort, not obstruction relieved by jaw thrust.

steps.x: **E. Tongue obstruction.** Hold the airway open and insert an oropharyngeal airway.

practice.stem: A 76 year old woman with severe COPD has been on the ward for 2 days with an exacerbation. She is now increasingly drowsy. Her respiratory rate has fallen from 30 to 7 breaths per minute. Her pulse rate is 110 bpm and BP 146/82 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of her impending respiratory arrest?
practice.e: A falling respiratory rate with drowsiness and a pCO2 of 11.8 kPa in COPD is exhausted, hypercapnic (type 2) respiratory failure: a cause of respiratory arrest.

steps.x: What is causing her to stop breathing?
A tiring COPD patient; the ABG shows high CO2 and acidosis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Hypercapnic respiratory failure** (CO2 narcosis).

elim: No glucose problem is suggested; CO2 explains the drowsiness.
Pneumothorax gives sudden pain and one-sided signs.
PE gives a low pCO2, not a high one.
No focal neurological signs.

steps.x: **A. Hypercapnic respiratory failure.** A falling RR in a tired patient is a pre-arrest sign.

practice.stem: A 44 year old man has been intubated after a respiratory arrest from a heroin overdose. The anaesthetist sees the tube pass through the vocal cords. His pulse rate is 88 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg.
practice.q: Which finding most reliably confirms correct tracheal placement of the tube?
o: Tube depth of 22 cm at the teeth
practice.e: A sustained end-tidal CO2 trace on capnography confirms tracheal placement, as CO2 only comes reliably from ventilated lungs. Chest rise and condensation can occur with an oesophageal tube.

steps.x: Which single finding is most reliable?

clues: sees the tube pass through the vocal cords
steps.x: Even visual confirmation needs objective proof.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: A sustained **capnography** trace.

elim: Chest rise can be misleading.
Condensation also occurs in oesophageal tubes.
SpO2 may stay normal for minutes after preoxygenation.
Depth helps avoid bronchial intubation, not oesophageal.

steps.x: **D. Sustained end-tidal CO2.** The gold standard.

practice.stem: A 26 year old woman is ventilated with a bag-valve mask after being found apnoeic following a suspected overdose. She now has a pulse rate of 98 bpm, BP 112/70 mmHg and oxygen saturation 92% on high-flow oxygen.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation to assess her ventilation?
practice.e: An ABG is first-line, giving pCO2 (ventilation), pO2 and pH. Pulse oximetry does not show CO2 retention.

steps.x: Initial test for ventilation.
SpO2 looks acceptable on oxygen but says nothing about CO2.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: CXR looks for aspiration but does not measure ventilation.
CT head is guided by suspected head injury or stroke.
Peak flow needs a conscious, cooperative patient.
Spirometry also needs cooperation.

steps.x: **A. ABG.** Plus a toxicology screen for the overdose.

practice.stem: A 31 year old man is found unresponsive in a park. His respiratory rate is 3 breaths per minute, pulse rate 60 bpm, BP 100/64 mmHg and oxygen saturation 74% breathing air. His pupils are pinpoint. His airway has been opened and bag-valve-mask ventilation with high-flow oxygen started.
practice.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
practice.e: Opioid-induced respiratory arrest: naloxone is given alongside ventilation. Naltrexone is oral and for relapse prevention; flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines.

steps.x: 'Next' step: airway and breathing are already done.

clues: respiratory rate is 3 breaths per minute
bag-valve-mask ventilation with high-flow oxygen started
steps.x: Opioid toxicity, already being ventilated.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **IV naloxone**.

elim: Glucagon treats hypoglycaemia or beta-blocker overdose.
Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines and can cause seizures.
Thiamine is for Wernicke's encephalopathy.
Naltrexone is oral maintenance therapy.

steps.x: **C. IV naloxone.** Keep ventilating until breathing returns.

practice.stem: A 24 year old motorcyclist is thrown from his bike at speed. He is unresponsive with noisy, obstructed breathing and then stops breathing. His pulse rate is 118 bpm and BP 108/70 mmHg. There is a scalp laceration and his neck cannot be assessed.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: With a possible cervical spine injury the airway is opened with a jaw thrust, which avoids moving the neck. Head tilt-chin lift is used when there is no C-spine concern.

steps.x: Initial management of an obstructed airway in trauma.
High-energy trauma: assume C-spine injury.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Jaw thrust**.

elim: Head tilt moves the neck: avoid with possible C-spine injury.
No opioid features; the airway comes first.
An LMA comes after the airway is opened, and is poor protection in a non-fasted patient.
Surgical airway is a last resort if other methods fail.

steps.x: **C. Jaw thrust.** Airway with C-spine protection.

practice.stem: A 52 year old man had a large meal 1 hour ago and then collapses after a fall. He is unresponsive and not breathing, with a pulse rate of 70 bpm and BP 124/80 mmHg. He is being ventilated with a bag-valve mask and has vomited once. An anaesthetist arrives to secure his airway.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate airway to protect against aspiration?
practice.e: In a non-fasted patient a laryngeal mask gives poor protection against reflux of gastric contents; a cuffed tracheal tube seals the trachea.

steps.x: Which airway protects against aspiration?
Full stomach and a skilled operator available.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: A **cuffed tracheal tube**.

practice.stem: A 3 year old boy chokes on a grape and stops breathing. Over the next 3 minutes his heart rate falls from 140 to 50 bpm before the grape is removed. His oxygen saturation is 60%.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his falling heart rate?
practice.e: Respiratory arrest causes progressive hypoxaemia and hypercapnia; myocardial hypoxia causes bradycardia and then cardiac arrest, the typical pattern in children.

steps.x: A mechanism: why does the heart slow?
A child with airway obstruction and worsening hypoxia.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Myocardial hypoxia** causing bradycardia: respiratory-then-cardiac arrest.

elim: Coronary thrombosis is not a cause in a healthy child.
Nothing suggests hyperkalaemia.
No trauma or ventilation to cause a pneumothorax.
A vagal reflex is sudden, not a progressive fall with hypoxia.

steps.x: **C. Myocardial hypoxia.** In children, fix the airway and the heart often recovers.
